correctness.rationale: Direct expansion gives \(8F=(2x+1)^4+6(2x+1)^2+1\). Hensel lifting proves exactly two roots for every target \(1\pmod3\) and no unit-input roots for the other classes. At \(2x+1=3s\) a unique 3-adic square root gives a bijective isometric coordinate \(H(s)=s\sqrt{1+3s^2/2}\), reducing the singular image to \(1/8+(27/4)s^2\). Counting all roots of squares modulo \(3^j\) then proves every finite fiber and image cardinality; geometric summation gives density \(25/72\). The included exact exhaustive standard-library checker passes every target fiber for each modulus through \(3^9\), totaling 29,523 target checks; finite testing is not the infinite proof.

originality.rationale: Ding and Zieve, arXiv:2309.14979, full-text Lemma 3.1 and Theorem 1.3 establish the value-set count/sum for even quartics over finite fields, including characteristic three, but do not assert any ring-modulo-\(3^k\) image or the complete fibers. Finch-Smith–Harrington–Wong 2023 treats prime moduli p≥5 and Sun 2003 treats primes p>3. Published indexed claims about other three-adic and quartic maps involve nonequivalent input polynomials. Actual semantic searches disclosed no matching formula or \(25/72\) density. Global priority remains subject to unindexed or implicit broader literature.

value.rationale: The natural polynomial \(x^4+(x+1)^4\) is a basic adjacent-power Diophantine value problem. At the exceptional prime 3, one singular residue class creates genuine higher-precision square obstructions not visible in the mod-3 image. The result provides a complete local-solubility criterion, every target representation count, an explicit all-level image census and the exact nontrivial local density \(25/72\); these are structural invariants useful for prime-power congruence problems rather than an arbitrary sample or a known prime-field table.
